query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) whose composition is tuned to form a stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitate (SCCP) microstructure (featuring δ-lamellae with coherent δ/γ interfaces) will exhibit enhanced ductility by promoting better dislocation transmission and reducing local stress concentrations.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten refractory HEA with a conventional dual-phase lamellar microstructure lacking optimized coherent nanoprecipitate structures.
generation.intervention: Systematic compositional adjustments via combinatorial alloy synthesis that promote the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates (SCCPs) and corresponding δ-lamellae features.
generation.conditions: Testing under ambient conditions and controlled cyclic loading environments to assess tensile ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent δ-lamellae and nanoprecipitate (γ) phases which create interfaces that facilitate planar slip and dislocation movement.
generation.mechanism: The coherent interfaces reduce stress concentration by enabling dislocation transmission (via shearing of δ-lamellae and interaction with γ precipitates) rather than crack initiation, thereby producing a favorable strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA with the optimized SCCP structure is predicted to exhibit significantly higher tensile ductility (in terms of percent elongation before failure) compared to a similar alloy lacking such a structure, while still maintaining ultra-high strength.
generation.baseline: A tungsten refractory HEA processed without inducing the SCCP structure, which typically shows lower ductility due to less effective dislocation management and greater stress localization.
generation.boundary: The observed ductility improvement may specifically depend on processing conditions that yield coherent interfaces; deviations in temperature or pressure during synthesis may limit the formation of the desired microstructural features.
generation.uncertainty: While the experimental evidence supports the role of coherent nanoprecipitates in improving ductility, the scalability and long-term thermal stability of such structures under industrial application conditions remain to be fully validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-based refractory HEA samples: one set processed to induce the SCCP structure via controlled compositional tuning and thermal treatments, and a control set processed under baseline conditions. Conduct standardized tensile testing under ambient and cyclic loading conditions, and perform microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, EBSD) to verify the presence or absence of coherent interfaces.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Microstructural analysis of phase interfaces (coherence, lamellae structure)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA samples with the purported SCCP structure do not show a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility over the baseline samples, or if microstructural analysis fails to correlate the presence of coherent interfaces with the observed ductility enhancement, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .
